#5726. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

#5725. Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

The news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on issues like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence shows.

Overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

Robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook said. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts said in the note.

The withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

#5724. First siRNA Therapy Approved for Myasthenia Gravis

— Cemdisiran is the second C5 inhibitor the FDA has authorized in a week

The FDA approved subcutaneous cemdisiran (Livsayis), a small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy, to treat generalized myasthenia gravis in adults who are anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive, Regeneron announced Wednesday.

Cemdisiran targets complement component 5 (C5), inhibiting terminal complement activation, a key driver of AChR-positive myasthenia gravis. It is the first approved siRNA therapy for myasthenia gravis.

The drug is the second C5 inhibitor the FDA has authorized to treat myasthenia gravis in a week, following the agency's approval of gefurulimab (Klygefa) last Friday.

The approval of cemdisiran was based on data from the 24-week phase III NIMBLE trial. For the primary outcome, Myasthenia Gravis-Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) scores improved from baseline by 4.5 points in the cemdisiran group versus 2.2 points in the placebo group, corresponding to an adjusted improvement of 2.3 points (P=0.0005). MG-ADL improvements were seen as early as 2 weeks after starting treatment.

A key secondary outcome showed a 4.2-point improvement in Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) total scores at 24 weeks compared with a 1.5-point improvement with placebo, corresponding to an adjusted improvement of 2.8 points (P=0.0015).

The MG-ADL is a patient-reported measure of disease severity and functional impairment, with scores ranging from 0 to 24. The QMG is a physician-administered evaluation of muscle function, with scores ranging from 0 to 39.

In the NIMBLE trial, adverse events occurred in 69% of participants in the cemdisiran group and 77% in the placebo group. The most common adverse event in the cemdisiran group was upper respiratory tract infection (12%), which occurred at a similar rate in the placebo group (11%).

Serious adverse events were less frequent in the cemdisiran group (3%) than in the placebo group (14%). No serious or meningococcal infections were reported in the cemdisiran group.

No deaths were reported during the double-blind treatment period. Two deaths occurred afterward: one, due to pneumonia, was considered treatment-related by the investigator but not by the sponsor.

Cemdisiran is administered subcutaneously four times a year and is available only through a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program, Regeneron said.

The drug carries a boxed warning for serious and life-threatening infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Besides gefurulimab, three other C5 inhibitors have been approved by the FDA for myasthenia gravis: eculizumab (Soliris), ravulizumab (Ultomiris), and zilucoplan (Zilbrysq). All carry a similar warning, and patients are required to comply with recommendations for meningococcal vaccinations.

People with generalized myasthenia gravis "experience profound muscle weakness that can affect how they talk, see, breathe and move, and with it their ability to carry out everyday activities," said Samantha Masterson, president and CEO of the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America. "This approval is a positive milestone for the [generalized myasthenia gravis] community, reflecting continued progress on outcomes that matter most to patients."

#5723. HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare

HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.

The company has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking. The company's FDA-cleared ECG detects signs of atrial fibrillation and allows members to share results with their healthcare provider.

Whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant. The company expanded its Advanced Labs testing—combining Quest blood testing, clinician reviews and AI insights—to non-members, alongside integrating Grail's multi-cancer early detection test. Whoop partners with health platform HealthEx to let users connect their medical records directly to the Whoop app, combining medical history with biometric data. A feature rolled out earlier this year lets Whoop members directly connect with clinicians through the app, including live, on-demand video consultations.

The company has raised over $900 million to date, including a $575 million series G round in March, pushing its valuation to $10 billion. Whoop told Bloomberg it plans to hire 600 people this year, a roughly 75% boost to its headcount, as it works to further integrate AI into its health and wellness monitoring tools and to expand internationally. The company is on track for an initial public offering in 18 months, executives told Bloomberg in August.

The company is positioning itself as a continuous health monitor that goes beyond fitness tracking. The device's 24/7 physiological data can function almost like an ongoing health check, becoming a bridge between everyday health and medical care, Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, said during an on-stage interview at HLTH on Tuesday.

Ahmed argued that the conventional annual medical physical is "frozen in time."

"The reality is wearing a continuous health monitor like Whoop that should be a 24/7 annual checkup. That's how it should function from a data standpoint," he said during a fireside chat with Michael Phelps, U.S. former competitive swimmer, who is the most decorated Olympian in history with 23 gold medals, and also a Whoop customer since 2015.

"Then there will be alerts when something is really wrong, and particularly as we combine these different data sources together, again, 24/7 physiological data, blood tests, medical records, how you're feeling and contextual cues. When we have all this information in one place, and now we've got 3.5 million members, about to be 4 million members, it's just amazing the insights that you can pull together from that. And so you can start to predict that someone may need to get a cancer screening, or may actually have a real heart problem," he said.

Whoop can pull together biometric data, labs, medical records and information to establish a baseline for an individual, recognize meaningful changes and recommend an action. By combining continuous monitoring with information such as blood tests, the company hopes to help users piece together health signals and determine when they may need care, Ahmed said.

For Phelps, Whoop has shifted from being about maximizing elite athletic performance to helping him manage his health, energy and recovery around everyday life and longevity, he told the audience.

"For me, for 20-plus years, I've been trying to chase time, and now I'm just trying to be the healthiest person that I can be," Phelps said. "For me, the data that I get every single day, if my body isn't 100% or I'm not full go, then I take a step back and I tone down my workout. When I'm talking to my trainer, I'm taking it down a little bit, so I have enough energy and I have what I need to be a good dad, to be a good husband, to be a good worker, hard worker, whatever it is, just to be a good person."

Whoop sees opportunities to turn deviations from an individual's baseline into actionable signals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Phelps said his Whoop device signaled that his temperature, respiratory rate and HRV changed, but he noted that the real benefit was that Whoop knew what normal looked like for him.

Using biometric data to recognize signals in a person's health can have broader implications, Ahmed noted, citing examples where members identified potentially serious health problems after noticing significant changes in their physiological data.

"We're just starting to see all of these different maps presenting themselves, and it's very empowering. We're excited about the role that we can play with the broader health ecosystem," Ahmed said.

Ahmed said Whoop's high user engagement and continuous monitoring can fill gaps between doctors' visits and provide clinically relevant information to care teams.

"I do believe that technology like Whoop can make the whole system much more efficient and also make a doctor's life easier if we do our jobs properly, which is again to say, how do you take all this information that's being collected about a patient or a consumer and how do you simplify it to the one, two, or three questions that a doctor might actually want to know the answer to before you show up to their office?" he said.

Ahmed sees the AI coach evolving into a personal health companion sitting on top of a longitudinal health record.

"That's another area that we're really excited about, where this idea that you can have a conversation with Whoop or what feels like this entity that sits on top of your data, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a health companion, and yes, you've got 24/7 physiological data from sensors, but you can also now have your medical records. You can also now have your blood tests. There are all sorts of conversational cues. 'How are you feeling today?' 'Did you drink alcohol last night?' Were you traveling?' You put all that information together, all that data in one place, and the insights are quite profound," he said.

Partnerships with other digital health companies and acquisitions help Whoop broaden the platform, he noted.

"We like to think about it from the consumer's vantage point first, which is to say, if you're an individual, if you're a consumer, what is data that you want on your body or you need on your body, and that may be data that's being collected somewhere else, in which case, we feel like there could be an opportunity for a partnership," Ahmed said, adding, "We're also comfortable now acquiring technology and acquiring different innovations, which has become more of a muscle that we've built over the last 12 months."

Whoop believes its biggest strategic advantage is the consumer relationship.

Members open the app roughly eight times a day and wear the device nearly 23 hours a day.

"There are so many of us who have been in health tech where we would die for that kind of engagement, and I think that's something we're always striving for because we're an industry that was never built with the consumer in the center," said Lynne O'Keefe, founder and manager partner of Define Ventures, who moderated the on-stage interview.

The company is strategically expanding into an older, more medical population. Whoop is a participant in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' ACCESS model. Ahmed said members 65 and older are actually Whoop's most highly engaged demographic, challenging the assumption that consumer health technology primarily appeals to younger people.

"It's clearly a population that cares a lot about their health. They want to focus on what's going on with their blood pressure, their ECG, or whether they need to send data to their doctors," he said.

Ahmed framed CMS' ACCESS model as a move from consumers simply paying for a wearable toward government reimbursement tied to measurable health outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure or weight.

"I think as a model of innovation for a government and its citizens, it's pretty interesting because it incentivizes companies to actually create technology or programs that are making people healthier. It should change the cost curve because you're paying if that outcome is delivered, and then to the consumer, you're both hopefully being healthier and not paying for a product that otherwise would have had to," he said.

Whoop also positions itself as a platform that can wrap around drugs and other healthcare interventions. The company announced this week a partnership with Novo Nordisk as part of the pharma company's redesign of its direct-to-consumer NovoCare program. Novo Nordisk relaunched its NovoCare direct-to-consumer program. Patients taking a GLP-1 can integrate wearable data from Whoop as part of their program.

Whoop can function as a potential companion for GLP-1 users, monitoring exercise, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and other signals while helping users preserve health and fitness during treatment, Ahmed said.

When asked about the future vision for Whoop, he said, "I think in simple terms, it's our responsibility to build technology that either makes you healthier or one day saves your life. You're going to have all of this health data on your body. I think organizing that information in one place, alongside 24/7 wearable data, and alongside a powerful AI that can sit on top of that data and go off on your behalf and take actions and schedule appointments with the doctor, or go speak to your doctor on your behalf, or alert you when something's wrong," he said.

He added, "God forbid this day comes, but you should wake up and be told from Whoop you need to go to the doctor in the next 30 minutes, and it's been scheduled, and you show up, and all of a sudden you find out that you're having a heart attack, or you're having some serious life event. To me, that feels like an inevitable future, and I do predict that a large percentage of humanity in the future will be wearing a continuous health monitor."

#5722. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#5721. Doctor's Mass Shooting Stuns Medical Community

— Colleagues never perceived Matt Lambert as a danger to himself or others

Doctors who knew Matt Lambert, MD, the emergency physician at the center of last week's mass shooting in Washington, D.C., were shocked by what happened, and said they never expected him to do something so dire.

Those who had interacted with him described a collegial, friendly person who showed no signs of any distress or any mental health conditions. Physicians spoke with MedPage Today about Lambert on the condition of anonymity.

One said Lambert spoke about problems with his condo unit, but it was "no different than if I said I was frustrated with a building problem. There was never any dark humor or anything that seemed off."

Nor did Lambert ever talk about guns, they said -- despite the fact he had at least three of them in his apartment the day of the shootings. On Nov. 12, he killed the building's property manager, then shot and wounded four other people before killing himself.

Joel Braithwaite, an attorney who represented Lambert, said at a press conference that he had spoken with Lambert not long before the shooting and said he was in "great spirits. ... I'm at a loss for how things took any sort of turn that would have us here today."

Braithwaite described Lambert as a "humanitarian" who helped people with scholarships for medical school. "He was also a great thinker, an author, someone who's very calm and collected."

Michael Brice-Saddler, a reporter for the Washington Sun, spoke with Lambert about a year ago about his ongoing issues with his condo unit. In a video posted with his report, Brice-Saddler said there were "no indications to me that he was dangerous or capable of violence."

"I went back and visited him multiple times," he said. "If I thought my safety was in question, I would have pulled the plug."

Last December, Lambert said this to Brice-Saddler about his ongoing condo unit fight: "It's affected every part of my life -- my sleep, dietary habits. I pride myself on my resilience, and I've been kind of surprised at how much it has been affected."

Brice-Saddler wrote that that Lambert did sometimes use "intense, combative language -- and at one point, his frustration veered into what at the time felt like dark humor." He made a reference to Luigi Mangione, the suspect in the 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare's CEO who is accused of inscribing "delay, deny, depose" on his ammunition. Lambert said those words described the condo association's legal strategy, according to Brice-Saddler's report.

Lambert also posted something similar last month on the X account he created for his unit: "After months of 'Luigi' tactics (delay, deny, defend) by the HOA, we were finally able to submit an independent engineering report into the record," it stated in part.

Brice-Saddler uncovered something else about Lambert in his reporting -- the sad fact that he was raised in Appalachia by a single mother who died of cancer during his first year of medical school at Marshall University in Huntington, West Virginia.

Physicians who knew Lambert told MedPage Today it was unclear if he had a partner.

It's well established that physicians with mental health conditions don't often seek help, which is particularly concerning given that doctors experience elevated rates of burnout, depression, anxiety, and suicide compared with the general population, according to a special communication published last year in JAMA.

Jesse Ehrenfeld, MD, MPH, a past president of the American Medical Association and a co-author of that communication, said that much work stands to be done on reducing barriers to mental healthcare for clinicians. That includes expanding confidential care options and removing intrusive questions on licensure questionnaires.

"We need to make that a best practice everywhere instead of just in a handful of states," Ehrenfeld told MedPage Today.

N. Adam Brown, MD, MBA, an emergency physician and healthcare executive who writes about clinician mental health, noted that "having letters behind our names as physicians does not grant us any special privilege of not having an underlying mental health condition," and that the U.S. needs to "take very seriously the health and wellness of clinicians."

"We also need to recognize the role that gun violence plays in our society," Brown told MedPage Today. "We need to take a look at both sides of the coin -- the mental health aspect, as well as the accessibility of guns -- to prevent acts like this in the future."

#5719. Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings

Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.

The investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing. The $28 million series A extension was led by MarcyPen Capital Partners, with participation from Pentland Ventures, Kinship Ventures, Hanwha, Gannet Capital, humbition and Comma Capital. Other angel investors also participated, including the Jonas brothers. The $200 million in growth financing came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions. It plans to launch more programming for metabolic health, PMOS, inflammation and immunity, and to launch a physician-supervised peptide program. It will add more diagnostics, including coronary CT angiography and gut microbiome analysis.

Hone also plans to continue building out its AI operating system that brings data together to help personalize care. And it plans to build out clinical trial infrastructure to support pharma partners.

“Longevity is thought of as this super exotic thing. […] I actually think longevity is now becoming primary care,” Saad Alam, co-founder and CEO of Hone, told Fierce Healthcare.

It costs $65 to test for 70 biomarkers with Hone, followed by a clinician consult with the option to add more diagnostics. Labs, health history, symptoms and medications are run through its AI, which then gives providers treatment recommendations. Hone can keep adding additional diagnostics and medications, per Alam, “and the AI gets smarter as we get more patients into that system.”

Additionally, Hone is publicly announcing Hone Black, a new concierge longevity membership that has operated in stealth for a select group of patients for the past year. It combines diagnostics on over 1,600 health markers with ongoing medical care from physicians. Offerings include prescriptions, supplements, peptides and lifestyle guidance, plus exosome and stem cell therapies.

Alam founded the company after experiencing a shift in his health at 35 years old, including mental health issues, depression and weight gain. His doctor was initially of little help. It took Alam a year to find out he had low testosterone, and after treatment, he finally felt back on track. That experience, along with his father dying from kidney disease and his mother going through early menopause, opened his eyes to the longevity space.

“This whole concept of longevity is going to be one of the single greatest problems I can dedicate my life to solving,” Alam realized at the time. He experimented with everything, from peptides to cold plunges to meditation.

Hone is a subsidiary of Time Therapeutics, which aims to support production of drugs that help people live longer. Alam, who started his career doing market research at Eli Lilly, knew clinical trials are expensive and inaccessible. He wanted to create a company that could help commercialize drugs. The first step to that is Hone, or a DTC virtual care company that can capture longitudinal data on patients. The next phase will be publishing research. Finally, Hone will look to partner with pharma to get drugs to market faster.

The company has been providing care for five years, treating about 200,000 patients to date. It requires patients to have a physician and get bloodwork every 90 days in order to get medication refills. Members can contact their clinician between sessions as needed.

“We make sure, for the most part, that you are doing bloodwork and talking to a physician, a real conversation with a physician, in order to get prescribed medication,” Alam said.

It isn’t about overprescribing medications. It’s about finding the most personalized protocol for each patient. “The companies that have—no pun intended—longevity are the ones that are going to figure out how to reduce the number of medications somebody might need,” Alam said.

Hone began with hormone therapy, then moved into longevity care with biomarker analysis and women’s health. Two months ago, Hone’s offerings for women surpassed offerings for men in terms of net new members. It soon plans to run clinical trials on poly-chronic patients as well to help determine the right drug at the right time. Hone crossed $100 million in revenue in 2025, per Alam, and is on track to double this year.

“When I started goop, wellness was a niche conversation,” Gwyneth Paltrow, founder and CEO of goop and co-founder of Kinship Ventures, said in a press release. “Today, it’s one of the biggest categories in the world, and the next step is bringing real health and wellness to the masses, not just the few. Saad has built Hone to do exactly that, with serious science and at real scale. That’s why Kinship invested, and we could not be more excited about what’s ahead.”

Hone will soon offer 14 longevity care categories, which Alam argues is akin to primary care. He estimates that Hone only refers to in-person care about 10% of the time, usually for higher-acuity conditions. Some Hone patients are already healthy; most are sick and willing to pay out of pocket because the current system has been inadequate in solving their health needs, per Alam.

“This is just the beginning of not only a way but a complete change in the way that medicine is practiced,” Alam said. “A lot of other companies are what I’ll call pill mills, and where we’ve really focused—our energy is making sure that we go through the more difficult work of managing the long-term health of our patients.”

#5717. Prostate Cancer Screening Is Changing. Health Systems Must Catch Up.

— Better preventive tools should be accompanied by accessible and affordable follow-up

For years, the medical community has been divided on prostate cancer screening. Urology organizations have continued to recommend prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing, while other societies and groups moved to emphasize shared decision-making and individual choice, after careful consideration of potential risks and benefits.

The American Cancer Society's (ACS) new recommendations incorporate updated data and make a clearer suggestion in favor of screening. Longer follow-up research has confirmed that screening prevents prostate cancer deaths, and advances in diagnosis and treatment reduce complications.

To support that recommendation, we must make the safer approach available wherever men receive care.

ACS now recommends a PSA blood test every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69, and annually beginning at 45 for Black men and men with a strong family history. Decisions at 70 through 74 should be individualized. Informed patient agreement remains essential, and screening recommendations generally stop at 75 or when life expectancy is under 10 years.

The strongest evidence for this change comes from the European randomized screening trial. After 23 years, men invited to repeated PSA screening had a 13% lower risk of dying from prostate cancer. The absolute reduction was 0.22 percentage points: approximately two fewer deaths per 1,000 men invited. One death was prevented for every 456 men invited to screening. That benefit is meaningful, but modest.

Screening also finds cancers that would never threaten a man's life. Reasonable experts weigh those trade-offs differently: the U.K. National Screening Committee recently declined to recommend population screening. Recommendations for earlier screening in Black men also rely substantially on modeling because trials inadequately represent them. Supporting the new recommendations requires that we acknowledge these uncertainties.

What strengthens the case for screening today is our growing ability to separate an elevated PSA from a mandatory biopsy, and a cancer diagnosis from an automatic, potentially debilitating treatment.

An elevated PSA should first be confirmed before further evaluation. MRI can then help determine who needs a biopsy. In the Göteborg-2 randomized trial, an MRI-directed approach reduced detection of clinically insignificant cancers by 57% compared with routine systematic biopsy. That finding supports a more selective diagnostic process, although it does not yet prove equivalent long-term survival.

Biopsy itself can be made safer. Transperineal biopsy reaches the prostate through the skin rather than the rectum (e.g. transrectal biopsy, which is the historically more common approach). In the PREVENT randomized trial, infections occurred in none of the men receiving this approach without preventive antibiotics, compared with 1.6% undergoing transrectal biopsy with targeted antibiotics. Cancer detection was similar.

For appropriately selected low-risk cancers, active surveillance can spare or postpone treatment. In the prospective Canary PASS study, estimated prostate cancer mortality at 10 years was 0.1%, and metastasis occurred in 1.4%. About half had received treatment by then. Surveillance means scheduled reassessment and intervention when warranted; its safety depends on continued and adequate follow-up.

Treatment is improving too. In the randomized MIRAGE trial, MRI-guided radiation with smaller treatment margins reduced cumulative moderate-or-worse urinary toxicity over 2 years from 51% to 27%, compared with CT-guided treatment. Bowel toxicity also fell. These results support precision in radiation delivery, while longer follow-up remains important.

In surgery for radical prostatectomy, the NeuroSAFE PROOF trial used rapid examination of tissue during the operation to guide nerve preservation. Among men with good erectile function beforehand, the approach improved erectile-function scores 1 year later and early continence recovery. Neither technique eliminates treatment harms, but both show that preserving quality of life can be a measurable treatment objective.

Aligning these advances with a safe screening program requires changes in how we deliver and pay for care.

First, insurers should cover the entire recommended evaluation without financial barriers: repeat PSA testing, appropriate MRI or biomarkers, and biopsy when indicated. A study of privately insured men found that median out-of-pocket spending for MRI plus biopsy reached up to $620 in 2020. A screening recommendation loses value when patients cannot afford the steps needed to interpret its result safely. Making this a nationwide requirement may take an updated U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation with an A or B grade, explicit protection for follow-up testing, or legislation. The task force's current C grade does not trigger the Affordable Care Act's no-cost preventive coverage requirement.

Second, health systems need reliable referral pathways. Primary care teams should know where to send patients, who tracks abnormal results, and how quickly evaluation should occur. MRI quality and interpretation require oversight. A negative scan cannot become a reason to abandon follow-up when other findings remain concerning. Regional imaging networks, specialist consultation and patient navigation can help extend expertise beyond major cancer centers.

Third, active surveillance must be supported as ongoing care. Patients need understandable explanations, dependable recall systems, and accessible reassessment. Payment should recognize the clinical work involved in monitoring a cancer carefully. Men also should have access to balanced consultations about surgery and radiation, including likely effects on sexual, urinary, and bowel function.

Finally, health systems need to measure whether screening delivers better outcomes. Quality programs should track unresolved abnormal results, biopsy-related infections, surveillance participation, treatment complications, and diagnoses of metastases. Results should be examined by ethnicity, insurance, and geography to identify gaps and guide improvement. Research programs should also expand enrollment of Black men in screening and surveillance studies, so future recommendations rest on evidence that better represents those at greatest risk.

I support the ACS recommendations. We now have stronger evidence that screening saves lives and better tools to reduce its harms. We need to make those tools available to every man we screen, with affordable follow-up, careful decisions about treatment, and support throughout his care.

#5716. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5715. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Tons of news coming from the nation’s capitol as Democrats set their agenda for next year, but it’s worth highlighting what else happened yesterday.

Epic officials publicly addressed whether their business practices choke innovation, as detailed in a STAT investigation. What did they say? Scroll down.

After the White House pulled its nomination of Heidi Overton for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday evening, the future of the agency that oversees $4.1 trillion worth of food, tobacco, and medical products is extremely unsettled.

The agency’s current acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, has reportedly said he’s uninterested in taking the role permanently, and even indicated he doesn’t want to stay at the FDA past the new year. Meanwhile, it is very unlikely that Congress has enough time to install another nominee before January, meaning that Senate Democrats will have final say over the next commissioner.

Who in the White House tanked Overton’s nomination? Who will replace her? Some people have suggested Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, or even a little-known guy named Marty Makary. (The former FDA head did not respond to request for comment.)

Where does this leave the agency? STAT’s Margaret Manto breaks it down.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is feeling optimistic about the first stage of his plan to vastly expand health coverage in the U.S. He predicted at a Wednesday press conference that Democrats will pass legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age while President Trump is still in office, and that Trump might not veto it.

Sanders would like Congress to lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision, and hearing care, and guarantee free Medicaid coverage to children until age 19.

And he pushed back on the assumption that Trump would veto such a bill. “I am not absolutely certain that Trump would not sign it,” he said.

The health committee does not have jurisdiction over Medicare, but Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), who is expected to lead the committee that does, said he is on board with Sanders’ plan. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) also supports the “Medicare for More” and “Medikids” proposals, an indication the party’s liberal and moderate wings are quickly moving toward common ground on a health care agenda.

Sanders also offered insights into the health care investigations he might undertake, including of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the insurance and pharma industries.

“Taking a hard look at the way the insurance industry runs, how they distort health care. Taking a hard look at the pharmaceutical industry as to why we pay by far the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Those are areas that need investigation,” he said. — John Wilkerson

Less than two months before he leaves office, Bill Cassidy took a stand.

The Republican senator from Louisiana rejected Jim O’Neill as the nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, cancelling the vote to confirm him over doubts about his willingness to stand up for scientific integrity.

The high-ranking health official had previously served at the Department  of Health and Human Services and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under health secretary Kennedy. But O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Kennedy in those roles, Cassidy said at a meeting of his committee.

More from my STAT colleagues on Cassidy’s bold move as his time in the Senate runs out.

At a panel discussion at HLTH, a health technology conference in Las Vegas, Epic’s executives for the first time responded directly to a STAT investigation that found the company is undercutting competition by selectively withholding data access needed by rival application developers.

Officials at Epic, the largest maker of electronic health records, defended against allegations of anticompetitive conduct and said they are seeking to build a more open ecosystem amid a deluge of requests for integration coming from third-party software vendors. They also said the company would make it easier for companies to use AI to read data stored in the company’s platforms.

Lots more juicy details from this panel, moderated by Brittany Trang. Read more.

In the wake of the midterm elections, leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement have said that their candidates were up against opponents with massive funding advantages.

But filings show that the movement’s political arm had more than $10 million to spend during this election cycle. Instead of directing those funds to promising candidates, it funneled millions to allies, associated organizations, and pundits.

One notable example: The PAC spent less than $50,000 on a California House race it called “the most direct ideological confrontation between the movement and its institutional opposition anywhere on the 2026 ballot.” It spent more money this cycle at Mastro’s Steakhouse D.C., a white-tablecloth spot that offers $110 porterhouse steaks. Another great story from our DC team.

Later this morning, a little-known but influential panel that recommends which preventive services must be covered by insurance will meet for the first time in more than a year, writes STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force will review recommendations related to cervical cancer, perinatal depression, and unhealthy alcohol use in teens and adults, all of which have not been updated in at least five years, and have been awaiting finalization since last year, when Kennedy canceled the group’s meetings and overhauled its membership.

#5711. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.
