#5635. Beverly Hills Penthouse Sells for $21 Million in Enclave’s Most Expensive Condo Deal of the Year

A Rosewood Residences branded penthouse has sold for $21 million, setting a record in the elite Los Angeles enclave of Beverly Hills.

After only 10 days on the market, Penthouse C at Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills has officially sold for $21 million, discounted from $27.5 million, making it the most expensive developer-sold condominium deal in Beverly Hills this year.

At $4,469 per square foot, the transaction ranks as the fifth-highest condominium sale in Los Angeles history by price per square foot. Only 18 condominiums have ever sold for more than $20 million in the city.

"It was a very quick purchase," sales co-agent Amir Ensani of The Fridman Group at The Beverly Hills Estates tells Realtor.com®. The median days on market is 57, according to Realtor.com data.

Ensani says the buyer, a man in the hospitality industry and his family, was—like all of the buyers in the boutique building—downsizing from a local "megaestate."

"The big thing that caught the buyer was a staff of 22 with armed guards," says the luxury broker. Additionally, the buyer, like many other high-net-worth individuals, was migrating to Beverly Hills in part because it has no so-called "mansion tax."

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

The buyer was also a fan of Rosewood Hotels, a global luxury hospitality brand. In New York, the company is behind The Carlyle. It does not have a Los Angeles location.

"It's like a double brand," the agent says about living not only inside of the full service Rosewood Residences but the separately incorporated city of Beverly Hills.

"A lot of the clients are Rosewood connoisseurs, including this one," he says. "They are accustomed to a level of service that Rosewood provides."

The Rosewood Residences is the only stand-alone residential complex for the brand in the world, a big plus for the property, says the broker.

"A lot of people who love the brand may not want a hotel component, with people coming and going," he says.

Another selling point was that the building is a "pedigree property," built on the site of the former Beverly Hills Friars Club, with interiors designed by New York-based designer Samuel Amoia.

"He likes to collect pedigree properties," Ensani says of the buyer. "When he saw it, he was like 'I must have it.'"

The three-bedroom, five-full bathroom penthouse blends sculptural furnishings, collectible art, natural materials, and seamless indoor-outdoor living.

It boasts nearly 4,700 square feet indoors and 2,200 square feet of outdoor space with 25-foot private pool and hot tub, as well as a custom skylit floating staircase, a double-sided fireplace in carved stone, and a private rooftop with a spa and an outdoor kitchen.

The penthouse comes with $18,740 in monthly dues (property taxes not included).

The amenity suite includes butler service, personalized fitness training, in-residence spa treatments, house car and driver, valet service, and private chefs.

Next year, the building will welcome two Japanese dining concepts, including a steakhouse and an izakaya (Japanese bar and casual dining).

Colisting agent Tomer Fridman says the units were designed as "estate alternatives" for affluent buyers accustomed to 30,000-square-foot mansions. (Sally Forster Jones of Forster Jones International & Associates at Compass also headed up sales at the complex.)

"These aren't pieds-à-terre with small galley kitchens," he says. "They were designed specifically for an audience that is accustomed to huge estates."

The smallest unit is around 3,200 square feet with around 300 feet of outdoor space, and they top out at 7,200 square feet with 2,400 square feet of outdoor space. Fridman notes it is only one of two condo buildings in Los Angeles with these types of "estate alternative" offerings.

The broker says the generous proportions helped account for the complex's brisk sales, which closed on more more than 50% in presales, a milestone the agency says is unmatched by another LA condominium condo building in the past decade. (The sales team wouldn't say the current percentage of closed sales.)

The estate-like units mean that downsizers can often bring much of their furniture with them—though Penthouse C came fully furnished and curated by the designer himself. Amoia previously designed the architect Robert A.M. Stern building at 520 Park Ave.

Despite the buyers downshifting from sprawling estates, Ensani says there is no singular demographic in the building. "We have families, we have people who are 20, we have people who are 80," he says.

While both agents agree that Los Angeles typically isn't a "condo market,"—with wealthy people historically preferring grand estates on large plots of land—it is becoming one.

Wildfires, the difficulty and expense of procuring insurance, and the expense and challenges of managing staff and maintenance, means that full service condos are becoming much more in demand.

"You have to show buyers that they aren't giving up amenities," says Ensani. "They are used to sceening and entertainment rooms. You have to show them they are gaining services, and someone else will take care of them for you."

Penthouse E, which is even larger than Penthouse C, spanning 5,817 interior square feet and 2,442 square feet of private outdoor space, will soon hit the market. The price hasn't been released.

#5634. When AI Pulls the Comps, Make It Show Its Work

Happy African American real estate agent looking at some leaflets of a house for sale

RISMedia’s September 25 Newsmakers roundup, “Tech Sharpens Strategy: Staying Ahead With the Right Tools,” asked agents and executives which systems are actually helping them capture market share and demonstrate value to clients.

One answer stuck with me. Veroushka Volkert of ONE Sotheby’s International Realty described using AI to produce listing remarks and email campaigns almost instantly, and also to pull real-time comps and list-to-sale data.

Those are two very different jobs, and I think our industry is starting to treat them as one. When AI drafts listing remarks, a mistake is cheap. You read it, fix a sentence and move on. When AI hands you a comp set, or a number a client will base an offer on, a mistake is expensive, and it usually isn’t visible on the page. A paragraph that reads well and a figure that is wrong look exactly the same.

I’ve invested in rental property for more than 20 years and own 50+ units across five states. Most of my expensive lessons came from numbers that looked finished and weren’t. One offering memorandum for a Chicago six-unit described the building as fully occupied on page two. The rent roll, around page 25, showed five of the six units vacant. Nothing flags that unless someone, or something, is told to reconcile the two.

So here is a simple standard I’d suggest for any agent or broker bringing AI into conversations about value or income. Before a number goes in front of a client, you should be able to answer three questions about it. Where did it come from? A comp, a vacancy rate or a rent estimate should trace back to a source you could name out loud if the client asked. “The model said so” is not a source. A rent figure delivered as a single confident point is also less useful than a range, because markets rarely hand you one number.

Was the arithmetic actually done, or approximated? Language models are remarkable at writing and at reading documents. They are not reliable calculators. A DSCR or a cap rate that is approximately right is worthless to a lender, and a buyer who relies on it finds out at the worst possible moment. The tools worth trusting read with AI and calculate with plain math.

What did it leave out? This is the question that protects investor clients most. In most jurisdictions property taxes reset at the purchase price, so a cap rate built on the seller’s current tax bill is overstated before the buyer even closes.

Roofs, HVAC and other core systems need reserves tied to their age, not an assumption that nothing will break. Who pays the water bill can swing expenses by $500 to $1,000 per unit per year, and it is often buried deep in the documents.

An AI that only answers what you asked will share your blind spots. None of this is an argument against AI. Agents who use it well are going to look much sharper than those who don’t, especially to investor buyers who expect underwriting and not just marketing.

But the question RISMedia put to its Newsmakers was about demonstrating value, and in anything involving money, demonstrating value means showing your work. The next time a system gives you a comp or a projected return in seconds, ask it where each figure came from, and whether you can change an assumption and watch the answer move. If it can’t tell you, that’s your cue to slow down before your client does.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of relea.ai, which builds underwriting software for multifamily investors and brokers. This letter is not about any one product, and the standard above applies to every tool, mine included.

Simon Asselin is the founder and CEO of relea.ai, which builds underwriting software for multifamily investors and brokers.

The "Choosin Texas" singer, 27, won entertainer of the year, female vocalist of the year, album of the year, single of the year, and song of the year.

When accepting her sixth award of the evening, she teased, "At this point, I'm sick of me!"

“This has been the most special night. I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life," she added.

At one point during the evening, fellow country star Lainey Wilson joked, "I said I was gonna bring you a bedazzled broom. I knew you was gonna sweep, girl.”

At the end of the evening, Langley posed with all of her awards as she smiled from ear to ear.

Langley will put her multiple trophies on display at her lakefront retreat, which she picked up in 2025.

In July 2025, Langley snapped up her first-ever home in her hometown of Montgomery, AL, just minutes away from her parents' home.

Langley, who lives in Nashville, TN, but was born and raised in Alabama, gushed about her newly minted purchase while speaking to Audacy, telling the radio station that she decided to make her first real estate investment in her home state because she feels most like herself when she's there.

"It just brings me back to who I am at the root of me every time I go back there. And when it comes to writing songs and being in that state of mind, I think it’s important to have a place like that," she said.

The star noted that, while she will likely "always" live in Tennessee, which is the home of country music, she will continue to keep roots in Alabama because of how close she is to her family.

“I think I’ll always have to live in Tennessee to some extent in my life, but being from Alabama, it’s so close. It’s under four hours to get there," she added.

Though many young people might find the process of buying their first property overwhelming, Langley conceded that she was in a much more privileged position—namely because she has her own business managers who helped to oversee the entire purchase.

"I honestly been having a blast. I have great business management. They just get all the phone calls, yes or no, this is what I want to do, and they figure out all the little logistics, so very thankful for them,” she added.

"The music family here is just really special; people are so willing to be a mentor or help you grow in a way I just couldn’t do back home," Langley said of her new home state during an interview with Raised Rowdy.

Previously, Langley has shared that her move to Nashville also helped her to find more freedom in her writing process, joking to Raised Rowdy that she spent much of her childhood in Alabama trying to "survive life" with two brothers.

"I grew up in the country in Alabama between two brothers, so a lot of my childhood was just trying to survive life between those two," she said.

"I always was trying to prove I was just as tough and fearless as they were. Being a tomboy like that, a lot of my friends ended up being guys. If you ask my band or people who know me, they’ll tell you sometimes I seem more like a guy than a girl. But I think women can still be direct, strong, and tough, without apologizing for who they are or how they think."

Making the decision to pursue her music full time was a serious one for Langley, who dropped out of Auburn University in order to focus on her passion.

“I had a boyfriend who was in music and then his manager, they were both moving to Nashville and we’re going to live with Trey (Lewis). And I was like, well hell, I’m not staying here," she previously told CountryNow.

"So I called mom and dad and I said, ‘Hey, I think I want to drop out of school and move to Nashville. I’m just going to be in more debt anyways when I graduate. I mean, I’m going to go do this anyways. I would rather start it now.'"

The singer also revealed that she was warmly welcomed to Nashville.

“It’s been a cool journey of finding those people for me in town that I just love and love me and believe in me and I believe in them. And so that’s what’s really kept me going a lot through this," she went on.

"And obviously my family supports me the way that they do and just love me, but that’s the thing, nobody has ever thought I was going to do anything else …

#5632. Lot Supply Rises for Ninth Consecutive Quarter

The supply of vacant developed lots continued to loosen in the third quarter as slower construction activity brought the national lot market further into balance, according to Zonda.

Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index rose to 88.5 in the third quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier and 3.9% from the second quarter. It marked the ninth consecutive quarterly increase in the index.

The index measures the supply of single-family vacant developed lots relative to the rate at which builders absorb those lots through housing starts. Zonda rated the national market “appropriately supplied” in the third quarter.

In the second quarter, the index sat at the boundary between “slightly undersupplied” and “appropriately supplied.” The third-quarter increase placed the national market in the latter category.

“The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” says Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market.”

Fergus noted that affordability pressures and widespread incentives continue to challenge builders’ ability to convert demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market indicates that lot availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction, he said, but does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost pressures have disappeared.

Lot supply increased year over year in every major metropolitan area tracked by Zonda except Boise, Idaho. Among the markets where supply increased, the average annual gain was 32%.

Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle posted the largest year-over-year increases in lot supply. Boise was the only market where supply tightened, with its index falling from 65.7 in the third quarter of 2025 to 51.9.

Despite the broader improvement in availability, 12 of the 30 markets tracked by Zonda remained “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed supply ratings during the quarter, Zonda points out.

Zonda also reported a modest increase in the future lot pipeline. Total upcoming lots increased 1% year over year and 1.6% from the second quarter.

Upcoming lots include properties in the later stages of development that are typically expected to become vacant developed lots within 12 to 18 months.

The increase suggests additional lots are moving toward delivery, although the pipeline is expanding much more slowly than the current supply index. The divergence reflects the role of softer starts in loosening lot conditions: available lots are lasting longer as builders respond to weaker demand and elevated mortgage rates.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5631. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5629. Thanksgiving Costs at Home Jump 6% in 2026 as Grocery and Utility Bills Hit Hosts Hard

Thanksgiving is the perfect time for loved ones to gather over a delicious, hearty meal. But in 2026, that feast could come with a higher price tag than we’d like.

According to the American Farm Bureau, the average cost of a 10-person holiday dinner will rise by 6% from 2025 to $5.86 per person. That’s because staples like turkey, milk, rolls, and cranberries have shot up in price.

And unfortunately, the higher price tag doesn’t stop at the grocery store. You may also notice a spike in your utility bills as your home’s systems are forced to work harder to keep everyone comfortable.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) found that the average family already uses over 300 gallons of water per day at home. With increased usage from additional showers, dishwashing, and hand-washing that are typical during the holidays, costs are sure to climb.

“Having guests over greatly drives up money spent on groceries, but it also drives up utility costs. Preparing all of that food often involves keeping ovens and burners running for multiple hours and using large amounts of water in both the cooking and cleaning processes,” explains Carrie Bernard, founder and recipe developer at Eating on a Dime.

Fortunately, it’s still possible to enjoy Thanksgiving without breaking the bank. A bit of planning and creativity can help keep your grocery expenses and utility bill in check.

Where you live can also impact how much you spend this Thanksgiving.

The American Farm Bureau found that the 10-person classic dinner in the Northeast is about 5% higher than the national average of $61.57.

Costs in the West ($58.74) and Midwest ($56.89) are closer to the national average. And if you live in the South, you could expect to pay around $54.33.

There are a few reasons for these cost differences.

“They largely have to do with supply chains, since different regions require different imports, and these imprints cost more the further they travel,” says Bernard.

Since the Northeast is generally colder, it relies more heavily on imports for many Thanksgiving staples, which leads to a higher cost for consumers. Also, the Northeast typically has higher operating costs for businesses, meaning that grocery prices are often higher.

“However, prices vary widely between different stores, and many of them offer special holiday promotions, so there are usually savings to be found,” Bernard adds.

While grocery and energy costs may be higher this Thanksgiving, these tips can help reduce them and enjoy the holiday without overspending.

Jim Wang, founder at Wallet Hacks in Fulton, MD, suggests exploring promotions at your local supermarkets and groceries.

“Many stores know consumers are being squeezed and often try to put out promos around Thanksgiving. They may offer the turkey at a low cost to get you to make your entire holiday purchase there,” Wang explains.

Depending on how you celebrate Thanksgiving and who attends your meal, a potluck might make sense.

“Every year, we do a potluck with friends and everyone brings something to share. This defrays the costs across everyone and while you don't end up with nearly as many leftovers, that's also excess spending you can avoid, especially if Thanksgiving leftovers don't excite you,” says Wang.

If you’re hosting, be a bit more conservative about how much everyone will eat.

“Sometimes we get concerned about having guests leave hungry and we make too much as a result,” Wang says.

It’s perfectly OK to make less of the more expensive items, like proteins, and bigger portions of sides that they can fill up on. Chances are your guests may prefer those sides to the turkey anyway.

Bernard tries to use her air fryer and slow cooker rather than my full oven when possible.

“These appliances are highly versatile and able to cook a wide variety of dishes, and they consume much less energy in the process,” explains Bernard.

Unlike ovens, which leak out heat and consume more energy the more you open the door to check on your food, air fryers and slow cookers cook things quickly and efficiently with low energy.

“I try to only use the oven when it’s required due to the size or amount of food involved,” Bernard adds.

#5628. Home Prices Hold Steady as Sales Drop and Inventory Expands

Home prices remained relatively resilient in October despite a sharp slowdown in sales and continued growth in available inventory.

The national median sale price was $383,598, down 0.4% from October 2025, according to the latest housing market analysis from Homes.com. Home sales fell 11.7% year over year while inventory increased 4.8%.

The combination gave buyers more choices even as elevated mortgage rates limited demand while sellers faced greater competition for the smaller pool of buyers prepared to purchase.

“October’s results tell a more nuanced story than the nearly flat national price number alone would suggest,” says Brad Case, chief residential economist at Homes.com. “Sales were down substantially from a year ago even as buyers had more homes to choose from, yet prices barely moved. That suggests demand remains strong, but buyers appear increasingly selective about which homes they choose to purchase.”

Single-family homes posted the smallest annual price decline among the property types tracked by Homes.com. The median price declined 0.3% from October 2025, compared with 1.4% declines for both townhomes and condominiums.

Single-family sales fell 11.2% year over year, while inventory increased 5%. Townhome sales dropped 13.5% as inventory grew 5.3%, and condo sales fell 15.1% while inventory increased 3.6%.

The figures point to a market where additional inventory has yet to translate into significant national price declines, particularly for single-family homes, Homes.com points out.

The relatively flat national median masks significant differences among major housing markets. Among the 40 largest markets tracked, 10 posted annual price gains of at least 2%, while nine recorded declines of 2% or more.

San Francisco posted the largest highlighted gain, with its median sale price rising 17.7% year over year despite a 13% decline in sales. Jacksonville prices increased 6.1% even as sales fell 14.4%. On the opposite hand, Austin recorded a 9.7% annual price decline, followed by a 4.1% decrease in Nashville.

Inventory trends also varied widely. Seattle had 22.8% more homes for sale than a year earlier, while inventory in Jacksonville was 9.8% lower.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5627. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5626. Hosting Guests Is Reshaping What Americans Want in a Home

Hosting friends and family may be doing more than filling the house. It’s also changing the way Americans think about what they want from their homes.

A new survey commissioned by KB Home found 58% of Americans say hosting guests has made them rethink what they want in their current or future home. The research, conducted by Talker Research, surveyed 2,000 U.S. adults in October.

Gathering spaces emerged as particularly important when respondents considered what makes a home comfortable for holiday hosting and special occasions. Open living areas led the list, selected by 35% of Americans, followed by outdoor entertaining spaces at 30%.

Kitchens also figured prominently. Twenty-four percent prioritized a spacious kitchen, while 21% selected an open kitchen. Another 21% pointed to a large or dedicated dining space.

“Hosting friends and family can highlight what people love about their homes and what they wish worked better,” says Gena Kirk, vice president of corporate design at KB Home. “From spacious living areas and open floor plans to finishes that reflect personal style, a KB home works for everyday life as well as special occasions.”

Having guests over also appears to sharpen homeowners’ perceptions of their existing spaces.

Nearly one-third of hosts, 31%, said entertaining makes them think about ways to make their homes more welcoming or comfortable, and 25% said it makes them want to declutter or clean more often.

The experience isn’t always positive. While 29% of hosts said entertaining makes them feel proud of their homes, 20% said it makes them self-conscious and 24% notice things they would like to change.

Shared spaces receive much of that scrutiny before guests arrive. Among hosts, 45% said they focus most on tidying the living room, followed by bathrooms at 35% and kitchens at 31%.

For builders, the findings reinforce the continued importance of flexible gathering spaces that can serve both everyday life and larger get-togethers. They also point to the role kitchens, outdoor areas, and living rooms play not simply as individual rooms but as interconnected entertaining spaces.

Talker Research conducted the online survey for KB Home between Oct. 9 and Oct. 13 among 2,000 U.S. adults with internet access.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5625. Chris Simms Scores a $4.5 Million NYC Home—Weeks After Selling His Longtime Connecticut Retreat

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has picked up a $4.5 million New York City residence—after offloading his longtime Connecticut estate for $5.5 million.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, recently picked up the property, which is located in Sutton Tower.

His new pad comes complete with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, and floor-to-ceiling windows, according to the New York Post, who first reported the sale. The property also boasts a chef's kitchen and panoramic views.

The Sutton Place tower was built in 2022 by architect Thomas Juul-Hansen. The residence is known to be the tallest tower on the East Side.

As a member of the luxe dwelling, Simms and his wife get access to a resort-style pool, a gym, a personal training studio, saunas, and a spa space.

His purchase came weeks after Realtor.com® exclusively revealed that he sold his Connecticut property for $5.5 million.

He initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately bagged a buyer for Simms' dwelling.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor plan that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now choosing to call to New York home.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

Simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving on to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the New England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

#5623. Mortgage Purchase and Refi Activity Hit New Low in Q3

Data for the third quarter for 2026 continues to showcase the effects of high rates and elevated housing-related costs, as the latest data reveals that the quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending.

ATTOM—the California-based property data and real estate analytics company—found that all mortgages and lending in housing fell in Q3 2026, in the latest U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report.

According to the report, a total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (one in four units) originated in the third quarter, which is down 12% from Q2 2026 and down 15% compared to the same period last year.

“The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” ATTOM CEO Rob Barber said. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.”

Barber—alongside other economists—attribute the third quarter’s cooling housing activity to the sharp jump in mortgage rates. After the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in September, the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.40% in mid-October, and has slowly decreased but remains over 7%.

Purchase loans fell by 9% quarter-to-quarter, for a total of nearly 730,000. The report notes that this drop is the lowest third quarter since 2012. Annually, purchase loans were down 12%, although the average purchase loan increased by 3% to nearly $412,000.

Purchase lending was also down in Q3 2026, totaling $300.6 billion or down 10% from last quarter, and down 10% on a yearly basis.

While activity declined, purchase loans accounted for 56.5% of all purchase and refinance originations, which is up from the 54.5% in Q2 2026 and Q3 2025.

Looking locally, 73.6% of the analyzed metros experienced declines in purchase activity. Some cities with populations over 1 million did see quarterly increases:

But even densely-populated cities were not immune to the effect of elevated mortgage rates, with these metros experiencing the steepest quarterly drops:

Alongside purchase loans, refinance activity fell 16% quarter-to-quarter, totaling 561,290 loans. This marks the lowest quarterly total since Q2 2024, and is down 19% from the same period last year.

The share of refinance originations decreased slightly, from 45.5% in Q2 to 43.5% in Q3 2026. Although not a significant drop in shares, refinance lending declined more drastically than purchase activity by city, falling 89.4% on a quarterly basis.

The cities with the worst drops were mostly in the South and along the West Coast:

Breaking it down by government-backed activity, Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans accounted for 15.7% of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from the previous quarter’s 16.1% and last year’s 17.9%. VA-backed loans were also down, representing 6.9% of originations in Q3 after the previous quarter’s 8.2% and 7.2% the same period last year, or the lowest share since Q2 2024.

Again, the 2026 housing market is shaping up to have a muted end, as pending home sales and mortgage applications have been on a downward trend for the past few months.

The increase in housing construction may spell some hope for housing demand, although experts did express skepticism based on longer-term affordability challenges and economic uncertainty.

#5622. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5621. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5620. Perez Hilton Returns to Miami Residence—After Hospitalization for At-Home Health Incident

Perez Hilton has returned to his Miami residence after a health incident left him hospitalized.

The 48-year-old was hospitalized in August following a distressing livestream that prompted several calls to police and requests for a welfare check.

Officers ultimately transported Hilton to a nearby hospital, while mental health professionals and the Crisis Response Unit offered support to his friends and family.

Hilton received treatment for multiple broken bones and significant blood loss. After undergoing surgery, he was transferred to an inpatient medical facility.

Now, his family has revealed that Hilton is “back with his family while continuing his recovery through an intensive outpatient program.”

They noted that he is getting "ongoing therapy" and "mental health support."

“Over the past few weeks, Perez has enjoyed several successful weekend visits with his mom and children. Being reunited with his loved ones has meant so much to everyone, especially after these past few difficult months. With Thanksgiving approaching, we’re looking forward to spending some much-needed quality time together as a family and enjoying a little peace and quiet during the holiday," the statement continued.

In September, his family shared an update on the situation as they begged fans to vacate his property.

The message revealed that before the livestream event, Hilton's "children, niece, and sister were inside the home."

"When it became clear that Perez was experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself, they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma," the message continued.

Hilton's family previously revealed that he was receiving medical care and was "able to communicate."

The update came after Hilton opened about his move to Realtor.com®, reflecting on what he'll miss most about his property and his fond memories of Las Vegas.

“It is a beautiful home, and it served me well personally and professionally," he said. "I filmed tons of television segments and news interviews from this home, and produced two documentaries.

"I would film every day for my socials, and livestream as well, and I do a lot of talking head commentary work. I filmed tons of specials for different networks and streamers in my home and outdoors. It's just so beautiful,"

"All three of my favorite spaces in the home have one thing in common—they are all very healing for me. The primary bath has the biggest, most luxurious shower that I've ever had, and the closet is huge and has so much space. Also, I never had my own, dedicated office before, and I really loved that. It's just the perfect home for a family. Everybody has space," he added.

Speaking about the property's location, Hilton told Realtor.com, "It was important for me to be close to the Strip, but it’s equal distance to Summerlin and everywhere we needed to be. My children’s schools, doctors, and dentists were all just a few minutes away.”

Hilton was especially pleased with the fact that his mother had her own private living space. One of home designer Blue Heron's signature features is a "NexGen Suite," and, because he bought the home before it was finished, he got to customize elements of the layout to ensure they were perfect for his mom.

“This was perfect for me, because my mother is a huge part of my family,” said Hilton. “She’s both grandmother and co-parent to my children. To be able to give her the space that she deserves was important. She had her own entrance, her own living room and kitchenette area."

However, despite his love for Nevada, Hilton noted that he is confident in his decision.

"It just feels like the right move, the only move, to make at this time. I've loved Las Vegas, but it's time to be closer to family," he added.

The property is being sold with Kathryn Winterton of Las Vegas Sotheby’s real estate agency, who told Realtor.com, "This home was designed for the way people want to live and entertain today. The natural light, open spaces, and seamless connection to the backyard create an atmosphere that feels both sophisticated and welcoming."

The home spans 7,000 square feet and boasts several modern living spaces, as well as a resort-style pool.

As in so many family dwellings, Hilton says the kitchen is the heart of the home, with its premium appliances, sleek custom cabinetry and a massive dining and prep island.

The kitchen opens up to the high-ceiling living and dining areas, which feel expansive, welcoming and luxurious. Generous walls of glass provide abundant natural light create a light, airy atmosphere.

Outdoors on the acre lot there's a pool, spa, lush landscaping and multiple outdoor gathering spaces. Hilton said he did a lot of his production work outside, as there are a variety of luxurious backdrops ideal for his commentary.

Set in a chic, private gated neighborhood known as Prado, Hilton enjoyed the fact that the home is on a corner lot in a small community with fewer than 20 homes.

Hilton and his family enjoyed the home, the community and Las Vegas in general so much he says he feels a bit of guilt moving his family away. But "kids are adaptable," he says. He knows this from experience.

A little over three years ago, Hilton packed up his three children and his mother and moved to Las Vegas from Los Angeles, the city where he had infinite Hollywood connections and a luxe, six bedroom, five bath classic Spanish Colonial built in 1926.

Prior to that, Hilton and his family lived in New York City for several years.

Hilton took to Instagram to explain the reasoning behind his move from Las Vegas, where he has been living for the past 3.5 years.

"We’re moving permanently to Miami. I am so excited, not nervous. I know this is the right move for me and my children and my mother," he said at the beginning of the video.

Although Hilton insisted he has "nothing but wonderful memories" while calling Nevada home, he claimed that his decision to relocate to the Sunshine State came from a higher power.

“I need to move to Miami for many reasons. First, this is heaven-sent. God told me to move to Miami. ... The holy spirit made these words come out of my mouth: ‘Let’s move to Miami,'" he said.

The influencer noted that his "trauma" from growing up in The Magic City has since been "released."

“My entire family is in Miami. I still have friends from high school. Though I have not lived there in 30 years, it has always been my home. Once we move there, any second now, it will feel like home right away," he added.

Hilton, who has three children via surrogacy, said a large part of his decision to move was due to his difficult year, which was filled with several health scares, including a 21-day hospital stay and a blood clot.

"Even though it was really painful being in the hospital and so sick, I reconnected with my faith, and this move to Miami feels divine. I was just listening to God. I used to not have a great relationship with Miami when I was younger, but now things are different and Miami is different, and I'm excited to get to rediscover it as an adult," he told Realtor.com.

Speaking about his health woes, he said, "I know this move will be great for my family. Nearly dying this year twice and the experience here—you never think it’s going to happen, but it was just so hard not only for me but my mom, for the kids, for my sister who is in Los Angeles. Everybody else is in Miami. To a new beginning and thank you, God, for guiding me back to Florida where my family needs to be.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.
